First measured results (provisional)

Source: vignettes/articles/first-measured-results.Rmd
first-measured-results.Rmd

Provisional. These are first results from two automated runs of the package’s pipeline (21 November 2026 and 22 November 2026 UTC) and one live test run (22 November 2026 UTC), on CDC AtlasPlus data as returned on those dates. Unless a section says otherwise, they cover HIV prevalence (people living with diagnosed HIV), ages 13 and older, for 2017, 2022 and 2024, with default settings. They have not been independently checked. The defaults they describe may change. Fuller articles with figures will replace this page.

This page reports what the package’s steps did to real data: how much CDC suppresses, what impute_suppressed() fills in, and what is left over. It has no code that downloads data. For what CDC’s numbers mean, see About CDC AtlasPlus data; for the tract estimates, see Extrapolation to tracts.

impute_suppressed() keeps CDC’s published counts as they are and fills in suppressed ones. The counts it fills in are modeled estimates, not counts CDC withheld; its cases_source column says which is which ("published", or the method that filled the count in). Nothing here says how large any suppressed count is.

How much CDC suppresses at county level

The more finely the data are divided, the more county rows are suppressed.

Share of county rows suppressed 2017 2022 2024
Not stratified 15% 14% 13%
By sex 44% 43% 42%
By age 50% 49% 48%
By race 60% 58% 57%

What the default imputation does

By default, impute_suppressed() estimates a suppressed county row as the state’s rate times the county’s population, and caps the estimate at 4. In 2022 the cap, not the state rate, set most of the estimates unstratified and by sex, about half by age, and about one in seven by race.

2022 Not stratified By sex By age By race
Estimates above 4 before the cap 77% 71% 50% 15%
Cases the cap takes off the estimated total 3,807 56,020 58,857 30,927

These are facts about the estimates. An estimate above 4 does not show that the hidden count is above 4. The column cases_uncapped lets you count the same thing for your own request.

Changing the settings moved the 2022 national total of published and estimated county cases by this much:

Setting Not stratified By sex
method = "zero" −0.15% −0.90%
cap = Inf +0.35% +5.28%
floor = 1 under 0.01% under 0.01%
population = "acs" under 0.01% under 0.01%

Stratified estimates against the county’s own total

A county’s count is often published while some of its counts by sex, age or race are suppressed. Adding up such a county’s strata, published and estimated, should give about the county’s published count. Under the default it often does not, in either direction.

2022 By sex By age By race
Counties with a published count above 0 (base for the percentages) 2,644 2,644 2,624
Strata sum to under 90% of the county’s count 717 (27%) 388 (15%) 273 (10%)
Strata sum to over 110% of the county’s count 112 (4%) 815 (31%) 386 (15%)
Cases short, added over all counties compared, misses of any size 22,763 21,241 17,590
Cases over, added over all counties compared, misses of any size 313 5,528 2,479

So stratified estimates under the default do not add up to the unstratified ones. By sex, 27% of the counties compared fell short by more than 10% and 4% ran over by more than 10%. By age, 15% fell short by more than 10% and 31% ran over by more than 10%. By race, 10% and 15%. Only the two percentage rows use the 10% line; the case totals below them include misses of every size. A net shortfall nationally does not mean every county is underestimated. Every county beyond the 90% or 110% line had two or more suppressed strata.

The comparison uses counties whose unstratified count is published. It leaves out counties with a stratum row absent, a stratum with no count (20 counties by race), or exactly one suppressed stratum (none in 2022). The two percentage rows also leave out the 132 counties whose published count is 0; the case totals include them. By race, a county can fall short with no suppressed stratum at all, because CDC puts cases of unknown race in no row.

Cases in state totals not accounted for by county rows

no_county_cases() reports each state’s total minus its published county counts minus the estimates for its suppressed counties. Added over states (shortfalls and excesses offset each other), after the default imputation and with the default no_county = "report":

2017 2022 2024
Sum of state totals 1,002,796 1,102,798 1,157,995
Remainder, not stratified 33,025 20,028 17,530
Remainder, by sex 51,988 41,696 40,514
Remainder, by age 39,541 33,238 34,698
Remainder, by race 44,429 33,659 32,382

In a few states the remainder, the shortfall of the county rows against the published state total, was a large share of that total in 2022, not stratified, under the same defaults:

State Share of the state’s total, 2022
Alaska 87%
Rhode Island 73%
Nebraska 60%
Idaho 47%
Vermont 19%
Wyoming 14%

Shares by sex, age or race are not shown by state: for some states they could come close to a single county’s count.

This is consistent with those states’ county counts being largely suppressed. The cause has not been verified. The remainder measures how far the county rows fall short of the state’s published total; it does not say where those cases are. County or tract estimates for such a state leave out about the share shown: most of the state’s total in Alaska, Rhode Island and Nebraska, and smaller shares in Idaho, Vermont and Wyoming. no_county_cases() and extrapolate_from_county() now warn when more than 25% of a state’s cases are in no county row, and name the states with their shares.

What CDC’s data look like inside a county

These come from the live test run, for HIV diagnoses and HIV prevalence. They are counts of counties that the run printed to its log. The run failed on a different check, so they are observations, not results of tests that passed. For the sums, it added a county’s published stratum counts and compared the sum with the county’s published count.

Where every stratum of a county is published, the strata sum exactly to the county’s count by sex and by age, in every year checked: diagnoses 2017, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and prevalence 2017, 2022 and 2024. By race, diagnoses also sum exactly, but prevalence sums to less in about a fifth of such counties and never to more. That is consistent with unknown race being in no row.

Prevalence by race, counties with every stratum published 2017 2022 2024
Counties 233 244 244
Strata sum to less than the county’s count 47 51 54

Counties with a published count and exactly one suppressed stratum cell are rare. There were none by sex, age or race for diagnoses in 2022, 2024 and 2025, or for prevalence in 2022 and 2024. In 2017 there were a few: 1 for diagnoses by age, 2 for diagnoses by race and 5 for prevalence by race.

What this means for users now

  • Unstratified estimates. The national total of county cases changed little with the imputation settings. That was measured nationally only: it says nothing about how much any one state’s, county’s or tract’s estimates change. In the states listed above, a large share of each state’s total is not accounted for by county rows under the default, and their county and tract estimates leave that share out.
  • Estimates by sex, age or race. Under the default, the county rows fell short of the state totals by about 3% to 4% of national cases in 2022, against about 2% without stratification, and by far more in some states. Individual counties can be over- or underestimated.
  • Report your settings. Say which method, cap, floor and population you used, and consider running the alternatives above as sensitivity analyses.
  • A better method is being designed. It will fit stratified estimates to each county’s published total. Until then, treat stratified estimates for counties with suppressed strata with caution.
  • Race denominators need a closer look. Census and CDC populations by race can differ for the same county; this has not yet been measured carefully enough to report.
